Chapter 7: Navigating High-Stakes Interactions—Negotiations, Interviews, and Conflict.
When things get tense—whether you’re in a negotiation, a job interview, or managing a conflict—your nonverbal communication matters more than ever.
In those intense moments, our bodies give away so much. Signals you might not even notice can reveal what’s really going on beneath the surface—hidden worries, genuine openness, or maybe even a chance for connection.
Think about negotiations, for example. Something as simple as shifting your posture or changing your facial expression can show whether you’re open to making a deal, or if you’re holding back. If you lean in, keep eye contact, and use open hands while you talk, you’re letting the other person know you’re engaged and willing to work together. But if your arms are crossed, your gaze drifts, or you suddenly go still, it might come across as defensive, or just plain uninterested.
Now, let’s talk interviews. Whether you’re the candidate or the interviewer, you’re picking up on cues the whole time, even if you don’t realize it. If you sit up straight, offer a genuine smile, and let your hands help tell your story, you’ll come across as both confident and enthusiastic. On the flip side, when the interviewer nods, jots down notes, or even mirrors your gestures, those are signs they’re interested and engaged.
Conflict can really bring out strong body language. Raised voices, clenched fists, or stepping into someone’s personal space—those are all signs things are heating up. But if you take a deep breath, keep your posture open, and use gentle gestures, you can actually help calm things down and rebuild trust. Spotting these signals in yourself—and in others—can make tough conversations a lot easier to navigate.
So, what can you actually do in these high-stakes situations? Here are a few strategies to keep in your back pocket:
First, regulate your own signals. Slow, open gestures and steady breathing not only help you feel calm, but they show others you’re confident and collected.
Next, acknowledge discomfort. If you notice tension in the room, don’t ignore it—gently bringing it up can actually build trust and open the door for real conversation.
And finally, try positive mirroring. Subtly matching the other person’s posture or gestures can help build rapport and make things feel a little less tense.
By using these simple techniques, you can turn even the toughest interactions into opportunities for understanding and teamwork. Remember, nonverbal cues aren’t just signals—they’re a bridge to better communication.
